items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 1972, British computer scientist Karen Spärck Jones proposed a statistical method for ranking documents retrieved by searches.
• Her method, inverse document frequency, weights each search term according to how many documents in a collection contain it.
• A term appearing in nearly every document, such as “system” in engineering reports, does little to distinguish one document from another.
• A term appearing in only a few documents is much more likely to identify the relevant ones.
• Variations of her method remain central to modern search engines.
items.stem: The student wants to explain why inverse document frequency gives rare search terms more weight than common ones. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Proposed by British computer scientist Karen Spärck Jones in 1972, inverse document frequency weights each search term according to how many documents in a collection contain it.
Because a term such as “system” appears in only a few engineering reports, inverse document frequency gives it more weight, making relevant reports easier to identify.
A term such as “system” appears in nearly every engineering report, while other terms appear in only a few documents.
Inverse document frequency weights rare terms more heavily because they are far better than common terms at singling out the relevant documents.
items.explanation: The goal asks why rare terms get more weight. The notes say a common term “does little to distinguish one document from another,” while a term appearing in only a few documents “is much more likely to identify the relevant ones.” Choice D gives that reason in its own words and links it to how the method weights rare terms.

A.recipe: OG (what the method is and who proposed it)
A.why_wrong: It says what inverse document frequency does and who proposed it but never explains why rare terms should count for more.

B.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: misattaches the common-term example to rare terms)
B.why_wrong: It has the shape of an explanation, but it misstates the notes: “system” is their example of a term appearing “in nearly every document,” one that “does little to distinguish one document from another,” not a rare term.

C.recipe: LIST (both facts, no link to weighting)
C.why_wrong: It sets common and rare terms side by side but never says why the difference matters for finding relevant documents or how the method weights them.

items.notes: Subject: technology (Karen Spärck Jones and inverse document frequency, 1972; well-known facts only, no invented details). Band 6: the goal states the weighting rule, and the key supplies the reason from two bullets; one goal-shaped FALSE (B reverses the weighting), one LIST in the manner of 3.2 C, one OG description.

band7.why: Planned band 6. Why-goal whose key derives the reason from bullets 3 and 4; after the fix one goal-shaped FALSE (B, caught only by checking bullet 3), one LIST (C, as 3.2 C) and one OG (A). One FALSE option is the band-6 count (band 7 wants two).

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In the 1990s, legal scholar Michael Heller observed that many storefronts in Moscow remained unoccupied.
• Meanwhile, makeshift metal kiosks on the sidewalks in front of them were stocked with merchandise.
• Heller discovered that for each storefront, multiple government agencies held a right to block its use.
• He called this situation a “tragedy of the anticommons.”
• He later argued that biomedical research could be slowed similarly when numerous patent holders must each grant permission.
items.stem: The student wants to make and support a generalization about the tragedy of the anticommons. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish these goals?
options: In the 1990s, many storefronts in Moscow remained unoccupied while metal kiosks in front of them were stocked with merchandise, since multiple agencies could block the use of each storefront.
In a tragedy of the anticommons, a resource can go unused because too many parties are able to block its use, as with Moscow’s unoccupied storefronts in the 1990s.
Heller argued that a tragedy of the anticommons could slow biomedical research when numerous patent holders must each grant permission.
A tragedy of the anticommons occurs when a resource is overused because no one is able to block its use, as the well-stocked kiosks of 1990s Moscow show.
items.explanation: A generalization must cover the tragedy of the anticommons as a whole, and support must come from a case. The notes say that for each Moscow storefront “multiple government agencies held a right to block its use” and that the storefronts “remained unoccupied.” Choice B states the general pattern (a resource goes unused when too many parties can block it) and supports it with the storefronts.

A.why_wrong: It describes the Moscow case accurately but makes no general claim about the tragedy of the anticommons.

C.recipe: PART (one further case, no generalization or support)
C.why_wrong: It reports Heller’s argument about one field, biomedical research, without making a general claim or supporting one with evidence from the notes.

D.why_wrong: It has the shape of a supported generalization, but the notes describe resources left unused because several parties could block them, not resources overused because no one could; the kiosks were not the anticommons case.

items.notes: Subject: social science (Michael Heller, “The Tragedy of the Anticommons,” Harvard Law Review 1998; Moscow storefronts and kiosks, and Heller and Eisenberg’s 1998 biomedical patents argument; well-known facts only). Band 6 make-and-support shape: one support-only and one claim-without-support option, plus a goal-shaped FALSE that swaps in the tragedy-of-the-commons pattern.

band7.why: Planned band 6. Make-and-support GEN as in 622a351d and 0acc26b2: support-only (A), a further case without the general claim (C), and a goal-shaped FALSE that swaps in the commons pattern (D); the generalization does not climb a level, so not band 7.

items.subtype: Describe a work to an audience familiar with its technique
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In stop-motion animation, objects are moved slightly between photographed frames, so they seem to move when the film plays.
• Władysław Starewicz was a Polish Russian filmmaker who began his career producing nature documentaries.
• When live beetles became inactive under his intense studio lighting, he started animating preserved specimens instead.
• His 1912 stop-motion film The Cameraman’s Revenge stars preserved insects.
• In it, a grasshopper cameraman secretly films a beetle’s affair with a dragonfly, then screens the footage in a cinema.
items.stem: The student wants to describe The Cameraman’s Revenge to an audience already familiar with stop-motion animation. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Starewicz’s 1912 stop-motion film The Cameraman’s Revenge stars preserved insects, including a grasshopper cameraman who secretly films a beetle’s affair with a dragonfly.
In The Cameraman’s Revenge (1912), Starewicz moved preserved insects slightly between photographed frames so that they seemed to move, telling of a grasshopper who films a beetle’s affair.
Starewicz, a Polish Russian filmmaker, began animating preserved beetles when live ones became inactive under his intense studio lighting.
The Cameraman’s Revenge is a stop-motion film, meaning that its insect characters were moved slightly between photographed frames so they would seem to move when the film played.
items.explanation: An audience familiar with stop-motion animation needs no explanation of the technique, only a description of the film. Choice A names the film and its year, notes that it “stars preserved insects,” and summarizes its story of a grasshopper cameraman who “secretly films a beetle’s affair with a dragonfly,” using the term stop-motion without defining it.

B.why_wrong: It describes the film, but it also explains how stop-motion works (insects moved “slightly between photographed frames”), which this audience already knows.

C.recipe: OG (how Starewicz began, not the film)
C.why_wrong: It explains why Starewicz started animating preserved beetles but says nothing about The Cameraman’s Revenge.

D.recipe: AUD (re-explains the technique, little on the film)
D.why_wrong: It spends the sentence defining stop-motion for an audience that already knows it and gives almost nothing of the film’s content.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Władysław Starewicz, The Cameraman’s Revenge, 1912; well-known facts only). While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Horticulturist Lue Gim Gong immigrated from southern China to the US as a teenager.
• In Massachusetts, he lived with the family of his Sunday school teacher, Fannie Burlingame.
• He later settled in DeLand, Florida, where Burlingame and her sister owned property.
• In 1888, he crossbred two orange varieties, producing a sweet, frost-tolerant orange.
• In 1911, the American Pomological Society awarded his orange its Wilder Medal, the first presented for a citrus fruit.
items.stem: The student wants to identify an accomplishment of Lue Gim Gong. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Having immigrated from southern China as a teenager, horticulturist Lue Gim Gong lived in Massachusetts with the family of his Sunday school teacher, Fannie Burlingame.
Lue Gim Gong settled in DeLand, Florida, where his Sunday school teacher, Fannie Burlingame, and her sister owned property.
Lue Gim Gong produced a sweet, frost-tolerant orange that in 1911 became the first citrus fruit to win the American Pomological Society’s Wilder Medal.
In 1911, Lue Gim Gong became the first horticulturist to receive the American Pomological Society’s Wilder Medal.
items.explanation: The notes say Lue crossbred two varieties, “producing a sweet, frost-tolerant orange,” and that the American Pomological Society awarded the orange “its Wilder Medal, the first presented for a citrus fruit.” Choice C identifies this accomplishment accurately.

A.why_wrong: It gives facts about where and with whom Lue lived but no accomplishment.

B.why_wrong: It says where Lue settled and who owned property there, which is not an accomplishment.

D.recipe: FALSE (scope shift: first citrus fruit becomes first horticulturist)
D.why_wrong: It misstates the notes: the orange was the first citrus fruit to receive the medal, not Lue the first horticulturist to receive it.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A rod spinning upright in a liquid alters the shape of the liquid’s surface.
• In water, the surface dips downward near the rod as the water is flung outward.
• In certain polymer solutions, which contain extremely long molecules, the surface climbs up the rod.
• This phenomenon is called the Weissenberg effect, after physicist Karl Weissenberg.
• The long molecules stretch as they wrap around the rotating rod, squeezing the liquid toward it.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between how water and polymer solutions respond to a spinning rod. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: When a rod spins upright in them, water and polymer solutions do not respond in quite the same way.
While water dips downward near a spinning rod, certain polymer solutions climb up it.
In the Weissenberg effect, long molecules in certain polymer solutions stretch as they wrap around a rotating rod, squeezing the liquid toward it.
Both water and polymer solutions change the shape of their surfaces when a rod spins upright in them.
items.explanation: The notes say that in water “the surface dips downward near the rod,” while in certain polymer solutions “the surface climbs up the rod.” Choice B contrasts the two responses directly.

A.recipe: VAGUE (says they differ without saying how)
A.why_wrong: It claims the liquids respond differently but never says what either one does.

C.why_wrong: It explains what happens in polymer solutions but leaves water out, so there is no difference to emphasize.

D.why_wrong: It states something the two liquids have in common rather than a difference.

items.notes: Subject: science (the Weissenberg effect, rod climbing in polymer fluids; textbook physics, no named study). Key is the shortest option.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Tatreez is a Palestinian embroidery tradition often used to decorate women’s dresses.
• Styles vary by region, so a dress’s embroidery can show where its maker lived.
• Dresses from Ramallah are usually decorated in cross-stitch, in which tiny X-shaped stitches form geometric patterns.
• Dresses from Bethlehem are known for couching, in which silk or metallic cords are laid on the fabric and stitched down.
• Couching lets embroiderers create curving floral designs.
items.stem: The student wants to contrast the embroidery techniques typical of dresses from Ramallah and Bethlehem. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Because tatreez styles vary from region to region, the embroidery on a Palestinian woman’s dress can show where its maker lived.
Bethlehem embroiderers use couching, laying silk or metallic cords on the fabric and stitching them down to create curving floral designs.
Dresses from both Ramallah and Bethlehem are decorated with tatreez, though each of the two cities has its own regional style.
Dresses from Ramallah are usually decorated in cross-stitch, whereas those from Bethlehem are known for couching.
items.explanation: The notes say Ramallah dresses “are usually decorated in cross-stitch” and Bethlehem dresses “are known for couching.” Choice D sets the two techniques against each other with “whereas.”

A.why_wrong: It explains why regional styles matter but names neither city’s technique.

B.why_wrong: It describes couching in Bethlehem but says nothing about Ramallah, so nothing is contrasted.

C.recipe: VAGUE (says the styles differ without saying how)
C.why_wrong: It notes that each city has its own style but never names the techniques that differ.

items.notes: Subject: arts and culture (Palestinian tatreez; Ramallah cross-stitch and Bethlehem couching are standard descriptions in textile collections).

• Hula is a Hawaiian dance form that tells stories through movement.
• Hula kahiko, the older style, is performed to chanting accompanied by percussion instruments such as the ipu, a gourd drum.
• Hula ʻauana, a newer style that developed under Western influence, is performed to songs played on instruments such as the ukulele and guitar.

items.stem: The student wants to compare the musical accompaniment of hula kahiko with that of hula ʻauana. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Hula kahiko is performed to chanting and percussion, while hula ʻauana is performed to songs played on instruments such as the ukulele and guitar.
Hula ʻauana, which developed under Western influence, is performed to songs played on instruments such as the ukulele and guitar.
Both hula kahiko and hula ʻauana are featured each year at the Merrie Monarch Festival in Hilo, Hawaii.
Hula kahiko and hula ʻauana both tell stories through movement, but each is accompanied by a different kind of music.
items.explanation: The notes say hula kahiko “is performed to chanting accompanied by percussion instruments,” while hula ʻauana “is performed to songs played on instruments such as the ukulele and guitar.” Choice A compares the two kinds of accompaniment side by side.

B.why_wrong: It describes the accompaniment of hula ʻauana but leaves out hula kahiko.

C.why_wrong: It points out where both styles are performed, not how their music differs.

D.recipe: VAGUE (says the music differs without saying how)
D.why_wrong: It says each style has a different kind of music but never says what that music is.

• Around 1850, he constructed the octobass, a three-stringed bowed instrument about 11 feet tall.
• Because of its enormous size, players cannot press its strings by hand and instead operate a system of levers and pedals.
• Some of its lowest notes are too deep for most humans to hear.

items.stem: The student wants to describe how the octobass is played to an audience unfamiliar with the instrument. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

Built by nineteenth-century French luthier Jean-Baptiste Vuillaume, the octobass is a bowed instrument whose lowest notes are too deep for most humans to hear.
items.explanation: An audience unfamiliar with the octobass needs to learn what it is before learning how it is played. Choice C identifies it as a bowed instrument “about 11 feet tall” and explains that players “cannot press its strings by hand and instead operate a system of levers and pedals.”

• At dusk, a red rose can appear nearly black while its green leaves remain clearly visible.
